hypothesis.title: Value-Equivalent Bisimulation for Autonomous Driving Policy Generalization
hypothesis.summary: We propose learning driving policies using bisimulation metrics constrained by value equivalence principles. This approach encodes only task-relevant state features invariant to distractors like weather or time of day, while ensuring model predictions remain optimal under reward functions. We validate this by training policies in visual MuJoCo and highway driving environments with varying distractors, measuring collision rates and route completion against baselines using reconstruction-based or unconstrained representations.
hypothesis.gap: Existing invariant representation methods (ref-009, ref-001) do not formally guarantee value optimality under reward functions, risking performance drops when distractors appear. Value equivalence (ref-004) has not been applied to continuous control tasks with high-dimensional observations.
hypothesis.approach: We formulate a bisimulation metric learning objective that minimizes distances between states yielding equivalent Bellman updates. This is combined with a value-equivalence constraint during policy training, ensuring learned representations preserve reward-relevant state transitions while discarding irrelevant details.
hypothesis.evaluation: Compare against ref-001's viewpoint-invariant representations and ref-009's bisimulation-only approach on CARLA and modified MuJoCo tasks with dynamic distractors. Metrics: driving score, collision rate, route completion, and distractor invariance tests (e.g., weather/lighting changes).

refined.title: Value-Equivalent Bisimulation for Autonomous Driving Policy Generalization
refined.summary: We propose learning driving policies using bisimulation metrics constrained by value equivalence principles. This approach encodes only task-relevant state features invariant to distractors like weather or time of day, while ensuring model predictions remain optimal under reward functions. We validate this by training policies in visual MuJoCo and highway driving environments with varying distractors, measuring collision rates and route completion against baselines using reconstruction-based or unconstrained representations.
refined.gap: While ref-009 learns bisimulation metrics to encode task-relevant information and ref-004 shows value equivalence applies to continuous control (e.g., MuZero), no work combines both principles to guarantee value optimality while discarding distractors. Ref-009's bisimulation alone does not enforce reward function alignment, risking suboptimal policies when distractors appear.
refined.approach: We integrate ref-004's value equivalence into ref-009's bisimulation metric learning. The objective minimizes distances between states with equivalent Bellman updates under the reward function. Inputs: state observations (images/LiDAR), reward function. Outputs: latent representations, policy. The bisimulation distance metric is modified to include a value-equivalence term: D(s1,s2) = α·|Q(s1,a)−Q(s2,a)| + (1−α)·|f(s1)−f(s2)|, where Q is the Bellman update, f is the encoder, and α balances terms. This differs from ref-009 by explicitly penalizing Bellman update discrepancies.
refined.evaluation: Compare against ref-009's bisimulation-only method and ref-001's viewpoint-invariant representations on CARLA (ref-001) and modified MuJoCo (ref-009) tasks with dynamic distractors (weather/lighting). Metrics: driving score, collision rate, route completion. Ablation: ref-009's method with/without the value-equivalence term to isolate its contribution. Distractor invariance is measured by testing policies trained on one distractor (e.g., clear weather) on others (e.g., rain, night).

hypothesis.title: Value-Equivalent Bisimulation for Autonomous Driving Policy Generalization
hypothesis.summary: This paper proposes using value-equivalent bisimulation metrics to learn invariant representations for autonomous driving policies, improving generalization across unseen scenarios. By focusing on state-action pairs that yield equivalent Bellman updates, the method reduces reliance on domain-specific sensor data while preserving critical driving behaviors. The approach is validated on CARLA and nuScenes benchmarks, comparing collision rates and route completion against geometry-based fusion and end-to-end baselines.
hypothesis.gap: Existing autonomous driving models struggle with generalization due to overfitting to specific sensor configurations or environments, while bisimulation metrics for MDPs remain underutilized in policy learning.
hypothesis.approach: Adapt value-equivalence principles to construct bisimulation metrics that identify behaviorally equivalent states in continuous MDPs. Train policies using these metrics to enforce invariance to task-irrelevant details (e.g., weather, background) while preserving value-relevant dynamics.
hypothesis.evaluation: Compare against TransFuser, EMMA, and VAD baselines on CARLA Leaderboard and nuScenes. Metrics include driving score, collision rate, and route completion. Ablate metric components (e.g., policy set size, function class) to isolate generalization gains.

The 'overfitting' claim is unsupported as no cited reference (including ref-015) establishes that baselines like TransFuser/EMMA fail due to sensor-specific overfitting rather than other factors.

The approach also lacks details on how continuous MDP bisimulation (ref-002/009) is combined with value-equivalence (ref-004) - e.g., whether the metric directly optimizes for value-equivalent model error or uses a hybrid loss.

This would isolate whether generalization gains stem from the metric itself rather than architectural differences. Additionally, explicitly test value-equivalence by measuring Bellman error consistency between learned and true models on held-out scenarios.

refined.approach: Extend ref-009's continuous bisimulation metric to enforce value equivalence (ref-004) by training an encoder that minimizes the Bellman error between predicted and true value updates for state-action pairs. The encoder maps observations to latent states where distances equal bisimulation distances. The policy is trained on latent states, with an objective to minimize collision rate and maximize route completion. The key difference from ref-009 is adding a value-equivalence loss term that penalizes discrepancies in Bellman updates for behaviorally equivalent states.

Ablations: (1) encoder trained with/ref-009's metric only, (2) encoder trained with value-equivalence loss only, (3) full method. Measure Bellman error consistency (ref-004) between learned and true models on held-out scenarios to validate value equivalence.

By leveraging the value equivalence principle, our approach ensures that learned representations preserve only task-relevant state similarities, improving generalization in unseen scenarios. We validate this by training a driving policy on CARLA that ignores irrelevant distractions (e.g., background changes) while maintaining performance.

hypothesis.evaluation: We compare against TransFuser (ref-005) and TCP (ref-015) on CARLA with added visual distractions. Metrics include driving score, collision rate, and robustness to background changes. A synthetic benchmark measures latent space invariance to irrelevant perturbations.

refined.summary: We propose learning invariant representations for end-to-end autonomous driving by extending value-equivalent bisimulation metrics to continuous MDPs. Our approach trains an encoder to minimize distances between states with equivalent Bellman updates, ensuring latent representations preserve only dynamics relevant to value-based planning. refined.gap: While ref-009 applies bisimulation metrics to continuous MDPs for driving tasks (e.g., highway driving with invariance to weather/time of day), it does not incorporate value equivalence to constrain the learned representations. hypothesis.title: Value-Equivalent Bisimulation for Safe Autonomous Driving
hypothesis.summary: We propose using value-equivalent bisimulation metrics to learn latent representations for autonomous driving that preserve only task-relevant state features while discarding irrelevant distractions. This approach ensures the learned dynamics model is sufficient for optimal value-based planning without requiring pixel-level reconstruction. We validate the method on CARLA simulations by comparing collision rates and route completion against models trained with traditional bisimulation metrics and reconstruction losses.
hypothesis.gap: Existing bisimulation-based methods [ref-002, ref-009] focus on state aggregation without explicitly guaranteeing value equivalence for planning, while reconstruction-based methods [ref-005, ref-022] preserve irrelevant details that harm generalization under sensor noise or domain shifts.
hypothesis.approach: We extend value-equivalence principles [ref-004] to continuous MDPs by defining a bisimulation metric that minimizes Bellman update differences between the learned model and ground truth, using only trajectory data from expert demonstrations. The encoder is trained to minimize this metric while being invariant to task-irrelevant variations like weather or background changes.
hypothesis.evaluation: We compare against baselines using traditional bisimulation [ref-002], reconstruction losses [ref-005], and maximum likelihood estimation [ref-004] on CARLA's Town06 long routes. Metrics include driving score, collision rate, and route completion, with ablation studies on weather/distractor robustness. Success is defined as matching expert performance under domain shifts while reducing model complexity.

hypothesis.title: Pseudo-Simulation with Value-Equivalent Dynamics Models for Closed-Loop Evaluation

By training dynamics models to preserve value equivalence rather than pixel/state accuracy, the approach captures only decision-relevant state transitions, reducing simulation bias. Experiments on NAVSIM and CARLA show improved correlation with true closed-loop performance compared to traditional pseudo-simulation.

hypothesis.evaluation: Compare against standard pseudo-simulation baselines on NAVSIM metrics (PDMS) and CARLA closed-loop scores. Measure correlation between pseudo-simulation rankings and true closed-loop performance across diverse driving scenarios.

hypothesis.title: Pseudo-Simulation with Value-Equivalent Dynamics for Benchmarking End-to-End Driving
hypothesis.summary: We integrate value-equivalent model learning into pseudo-simulation to improve correlation with closed-loop driving performance. By generating synthetic observations that preserve value equivalence to real dynamics, the pseudo-simulation better captures error propagation. This is validated by comparing correlation coefficients with closed-loop CARLA benchmarks against standard pseudo-simulation.
hypothesis.gap: Current pseudo-simulation methods use physics-based or heuristic dynamics models that may not preserve value-relevant aspects of the environment, reducing correlation with closed-loop performance.
hypothesis.approach: Learn a value-equivalent dynamics model from real data that matches Bellman updates of the target policy. Use this model to generate synthetic observations in pseudo-simulation, weighting them by proximity to the policy's likely trajectory.
hypothesis.evaluation: Compare correlation (R²) with closed-loop CARLA Driving Score against standard pseudo-simulation (ref-010) and open-loop metrics. Test on NAVSIM scenarios with varying agent densities and dynamic obstacles.

Outputs: synthetic observations preserving value equivalence. Update rule: minimize the difference between Bellman updates under real and synthetic dynamics.
